system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2134-10-18 20:51:00 to 2134-10-19 17:03:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

History of Present Illness:
Mr. ___ is a ___ M with connective tissue disorder resulting 
in polychondritis developing acute respiratory failure s/p 
tracheostomy and multiple endobronchial dilations now with 
recurrence of LMS and BI stenosis. 

He was admitted early ___ with dyspnea and hypoxemia (in 
the setting of patient having stopped prednisone) then 
developing respiratory arrest after difficult intubation for 
attempted procedure to dilate airways. He had developed complete 
collapse of left mainstem bronchus as well as bronchus 
intermedius and tracheal stenosis. He was again admitted on 
___ for placement of T tube which was unsuccessful.

worsening shortness of breath, significant cough or mucus

trach humidification adapter. He then went for procedure by IP 
and head/neck surgery where he was noted to have recurrent 
severe airway stenosis with trach in place. He underwent 
dilation of multiple upper airways. He tolerated the procedure 
well and was on supplemental O2 in PACU while recovering from 
anesthesia.
 
On the floor,  patient reports he is feeling very well and 
denies chest pain, SOB, fevers, chills, joint pain, nausea. He 
is in no acute distress and is on supplemental oxygen with 
humidified air. He typically uses supplemental oxygen at home.

Mr. ___ is a ___ M with connective tissue disorder resulting 
in polychondritis developing acute respiratory failure s/p 
tracheostomy and multiple endobronchial dilations now with 
recurrence of LMS and BI stenosis s/p dilatation by IP on ___. 


ACUTE ISSUES:
# Acute on Chronic Respiratory Failure - Left mainstem and 
bronchus intermedius stenosis due to complications of his 
undefined connective tissue disorder. He is now s/p dilation of 
multiple upper airways by IP and ENT. His trach was exchanged by 
ENT on ___ who noticed severe airway stenosis requiring 
dilation by IP the same day. He was admitted to medicine after 
the procedure. His home dose of prednisone was increased to 60mg

continued on a trach collar with humidified air to keep oxygen

disorder with short stature, precocious puberty, contractures 
and pericarditis with noninflammatory fluid with recurrent 
stenosis in his tracheobronchial trees and multiple 
interventions and dilatation with inflammatory findings on his 
transbronchial biopsy suggestive of relapsing polychondritis. He 
was followed by rheumatology outpatient. Rheumatology was 
consulted as above. Bactrim was also started during this 
admission for infection prophylaxis as patient has been taking 
chronic 30mg prednisone and will be discharged on a steroid 
taper as above. 

# Leukocytosis - 19 on ___ after increasing prednisone from 
30mg to 60mg. Likely from steroid dose increase or from 
procedure the day prior as differential showed 92% PMNs. He 
showed no signs of infection, and has been afebrile. CXR was 
negative.

# Constipation - continued lactulose prn

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___, one of your hospital doctors. You're here because you had a procedure today for your airway, and we want to keep an eye on you afterward. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, doctor. I’m feeling okay. A bit tired, but no pain. My breathing feels a little easier than before the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. The ENT and interventional pulmonology teams found significant narrowing in your left mainstem bronchus and bronchus intermedius again, so they did a dilation to open those areas up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, so it came back? I thought the last dilation helped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because of your underlying condition—polychondritis—the scarring and narrowing tend to recur. That’s why we’re also adjusting your medications to help reduce inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, the connective tissue disorder. So what’s changed with my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve increased your prednisone from 30 mg to 60 mg for two days to help calm the inflammation after the procedure. Then you’ll taper down—50 mg for two days, then 40 mg for two days, and back to your usual 30 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can do that. But why the change now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because the procedure itself causes some inflammation, and with your history of stopping prednisone before, we want to make sure we prevent another flare-up like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I didn’t realize stopping it could cause such a problem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can, especially with your condition. Also, because you’re on long-term steroids, we’re starting you on Bactrim—one tablet daily—for infection prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve never taken that before. Any side effects I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most people tolerate it well. Just let us know if you develop a rash, fever, or any mouth sores. It’s mainly to protect you while your immune system is a bit suppressed from the steroids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your chest X-ray this morning looks stable—your trach is in place, lungs are clear. No signs of complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. My breathing still feels okay. I’m using the humidifier like always.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. The humidified air helps keep your airway moist, especially with the trach. One lab note—your white blood cell count is elevated, about 19.2, but that’s likely from the steroids or the procedure, not an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not in this case. You’re not running a fever, and your lungs sound stable. Steroids often raise the white count. We’ll monitor it, but no need for concern now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re getting ready to discharge you. You’re doing well—no shortness of breath, vitals stable. Just a few last things to go over.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the steroid taper as we discussed: 50 mg tomorrow, 40 mg the next two days, then back to 30 mg daily. Keep taking Bactrim daily, and stay on your famotidine and lactulose as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the humidifier?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, keep using humidified air with your trach. It helps prevent dryness and thick secretions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, rheumatology will help set you up on Enbrel after discharge. Call their nurse to arrange delivery. You have follow-up appointments with rheumatology, ENT, and pulmonology—someone will call you with the pulmonology appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll make sure to call. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You tolerated the procedure well, and your recovery is on track. Just monitor your breathing—if you feel more short of breath, let someone know right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. I feel much better than I did last time I was here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. You should be heading home soon.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for management following a procedure to address recurrent airway stenosis. He underwent microlaryngoscopy with balloon dilation and bronchial dilation due to severe stenosis in the left mainstem bronchus and bronchus intermedius, complications of his underlying connective tissue disorder with polychondritis. Post-procedure, he was stabilized on supplemental humidified oxygen and started on a short-term prednisone taper (60 mg for two days, then step-down) and Bactrim for infection prophylaxis. His white blood cell count rose to 19.2, attributed to steroid use or procedural inflammation, with no signs of infection. He remained in no acute distress, with stable vital signs and a clear chest X-ray. He was discharged home with follow-up arranged in rheumatology, ENT, and pulmonology, and instructions to continue trach care with humidification and medication tapering.
